newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. election to overshadow economics.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. election to overshadow economics.

text.p: U.S. elections will dominate the coming week for international financial markets, leaving economic data to bring up the rear, analysts said on Friday.

On November 5, the U.S. elects a president, vice-president, members of the House of Representatives, and other officials. A Reuters poll showed Democratic President Bill Clinton ahead with 41.9 percent, trailed by Republican Bob Dole with 34.2 percent.

"People have already taken it for granted that Clinton will win, but they are looking to see if there is a shift in the balance of power," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston in London.

"Clinton's hands have been tied in the past by having a Republican dominated Congress and Senate, but there are concerns that if that changes there will be a loosening in fiscal policy," said Shepley.
Analysts said the effects of Friday's non-farm payrolls which showed a rise of 210,000 in October and a steady 5.2 percent unemployment rate, would be muted by the looming election.

The quarterly refunding will also get underway with the auction of $28 billion of three- and six month paper, an $18.5 billion auction of three-year notes, and $10 billion each of 10-and 30-year paper.

In Europe, the Bank of England's (BOE) quarterly inflation report on Wednesday is a major focus for the market in the wake of the recent unexpected 25 basis point rise in British base rates to 6.0 percent.

Analysts said Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's decision to raise rates, after he initially appeared to oppose the move, may lead the central bank to issue a more positive picture of the economy, with little threat from inflation.

"The market is expecting the report to be kind to the chancellor," said Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets in London. "The risk is one of disappointment if the BOE doesn't budge from its usual gloomy (inflation) prospects."
Shepley said it would be hard for the bank to keep its inflation forecast unchanged, given the recent rise in sterling.
The last inflation report in August said it projected British RPIX inflation a little above 2.5 percent in two years' time.

Tuesday's British industrial production and manufacturing output data for September was expected to interest the markets. Industrial production was forecast by a Reuters poll to rise 0.5 percent, and manufacturing output was expected to show an increase of the same amount.
Germany was also expected to release September industrial production data in the early part of the week. The forecast was for a rise of 0.5 percent on the month, to give a yearly rise of 0.9 percent.
"German data is showing that a gradually improving picture is unfolding," said Peter Frank, senior economist at Sumitomo Finance International in London. "But activity data is still fairly weak."
Unemployment data for Germany in October was due for release on Thursday.
In Japan, there are few important economic releases scheduled, but analysts said the market was likely to be dominated by the prospects for the yen.
"The weakness of the yen will continue to be driven by whatever official comments are made," said Smith. "We are not going to see a sharp reversal."
Japanese trade data could also be released at the end of the week.
